ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, a smooth inclined plane with an angle of $\theta$ is fixed on a horizontal ground. Under the action of a constant force along the inclined plane, a block of mass $m$ starts to slide upward from rest. When the sliding distance is $x$, its speed is $v$. At this point, the force is removed, and the block continues to move. The inclined plane is assumed to be sufficiently long. The gravitational acceleration is $g$.

1. The magnitude of the constant force $F$
2. After the force is removed, the distance the block continues to slide up the incline is $x^{\prime}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, there is a small block located near the bottom of an inclined plane; the inclined plane makes an angle \(\theta\) relative to the horizontal ground, and the direction in which the block moves upward along the inclined plane is the uphill direction along the inclined plane. The problem states that the inclined plane is smooth, so friction is not considered in the direction along the inclined plane. Reasoning: Take upward along the inclined plane as the positive direction. In the first stage, the block starts from rest, and under the action of the constant force \(F\), after sliding upward along the inclined plane a distance \(x\), its speed is \(v\). From the kinematic formula \(v^2-0=2a_1x\), obtain \(a_1=\frac{v^2}{2x}\). The forces in the direction along the inclined plane are the constant force \(F\) upward and the gravitational component \(mg\sin\theta\) downward, so from Newton's second law \(F-mg\sin\theta=ma_1\). Substituting \(a_1\), obtain \(F=mg\sin\theta+\frac{mv^2}{2x}\). In the second stage, after the constant force is removed, in the direction along the inclined plane only the gravitational component \(mg\sin\theta\) makes the block decelerate, so the acceleration is \(a_2=-g\sin\theta\). When the block continues to slide upward to the highest point, its speed is 0; let the distance it continues to slide upward be \(x'\). From \(0-v^2=2(-g\sin\theta)x'\), obtain \(x'=\frac{v^2}{2g\sin\theta}\).
